transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

I'm seeking help because I've been struggling a lot with impulsivity, especially when talking to others. I constantly find myself interrupting people and blurting out answers before they even have a chance to finish speaking.
Besides the impulsivity, do you also have trouble paying attention, like making careless mistakes, losing things, or getting easily distracted? If so, has that been a regular problem for you?
No, I don't really have those specific issues with paying attention or losing things. I don't tend to make careless mistakes like that. My struggles are really just with the impulsivity.
Have these impulsive behaviors been present since childhood, or did they start later in life? About how old were you when they began?

Yes, they definitely started back when I was a kid. I remember getting in trouble for interrupting teachers and blurting things out back in elementary school, probably when I was around 8 or 9 years old. They've been a constant issue for me ever since.
Do these impulsive behaviors happen in more than one setting, like at work or school, at home, and with friends? Have they caused problems in those areas?

To be honest, I'm not entirely sure if it spans across all of those different areas. I haven't really thought about it much in terms of specific settings like work versus home, so I can't say for certain where it's worse.
Can you give me one example of this happening at home and one example at work, school, or with friends? Have these behaviors led to any arguments, discipline, or other problems in those situations?

At home, I constantly interrupt my family's conversations or butt into their quiet activities, which has caused some arguments and frustration. At work, I often blurt out ideas and interrupt my colleagues during meetings before they can finish speaking, which has created friction because they feel cut off.
Along with interrupting and blurting things out, do you also often feel physically restless, fidget a lot, or have trouble staying seated when expected?

No, I don't really experience physical restlessness or fidgeting. I don't have any trouble staying seated when I'm expected to, either. My issues are really just with the verbal impulsivity and interrupting.

Aside from interrupting and blurting things out, do you often act without thinking in other ways, like having trouble waiting your turn, intruding on others, or making quick decisions you later regret?

Yes, I definitely have a big problem with intruding on others. I often find myself butting into people's conversations, games, or activities without meaning to. I'm not really sure about having trouble waiting my turn or making quick decisions, though.
Do you often have trouble waiting your turn, like in lines, conversations, or group activities?
I haven't really noticed having trouble waiting my turn in lines or other situations. I'm not quite sure about that being an issue for me.
Do people often tell you that you talk excessively or keep talking even when others are trying to speak?

Yes, that is definitely a frequent issue for me. I often blurt out my thoughts or answers before others have even finished speaking, and I constantly find myself interrupting or butting in when they are trying to talk. It's really hard for me to hold back and let them finish.
How much are these impulsive speaking behaviors affecting your daily life right now, such as your work performance or relationships?

I'm not entirely sure how to measure the exact impact it has on my work or relationships. I haven't really thought about it much in that way, so it's hard for me to say how much it is actually affecting those areas.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a longstanding pattern since childhood of hyperactive/impulsive ADHD symptoms centered on verbal impulsivity and intrusion: blurting out answers, interrupting others, intruding into conversations/activities, and excessive talking. Inattentive symptoms were denied. Symptoms are present in multiple settings (home and work) and have caused interpersonal friction. Although the full symptom threshold for DSM-5 hyperactive/impulsive presentation was not completely assessed, the interview most strongly supports this diagnosis from the allowed candidate list.
